summary: Describes the optional AUTH command for POP3, which names an authentication mechanism, runs an exchange with the server, and can negotiate protection for later traffic. It has been replaced by RFC 5034.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for a mail program to pick a stronger password handshake than plain login.

questions: what does pop3 auth command do
subtitle: A secure way for mail programs to log into servers using stronger authentication methods.

tldr.problem: POP3 servers used basic username and password authentication, which was weak and exposed credentials.
tldr.mechanism: The AUTH command lets a mail client request a security mechanism (like Kerberos), then exchange credentials with the server using an encoded protocol exchange rather than plain passwords.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was replaced by RFC 5034 in 2008, which simplified and clarified AUTH for POP3.

today: RFC 1734 was replaced by RFC 5034 in 2007, which standardized the SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) mechanism for POP3.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: POP3 is a protocol that mail programs use to fetch messages from a server. RFC 1734 adds an optional AUTH command to POP3 that supports multiple authentication mechanisms. Instead of using the simple USER and PASS commands, AUTH lets clients and servers negotiate a stronger way to prove identity, similar to mechanisms used by IMAP4.
sections.plainLanguage: POP3 is the pickup window where your mail arrives. AUTH is a better way to prove it is really you picking up your mail.

sections.title: How AUTH Works
sections.content: When a client issues AUTH, it names an authentication mechanism (such as KERBEROS_V4). If the server supports it, a series of challenge and response exchanges follows, with each message encoded in BASE64. The client can cancel at any time by sending a single asterisk. If the mechanism includes a protection layer, all subsequent data on the connection is encrypted and length-prefixed.
sections.plainLanguage: The client picks a secret password game, the server agrees (or says no), then they play it step by step. Once done, all the mail talks are scrambled.

sections.title: Security and Fallback
sections.content: The AUTH command operates only in the authorization state, before the user is logged in. If an AUTH attempt fails, the client can try a different mechanism or fall back to USER/PASS. The RFC does not require servers to support any particular mechanism, and protection mechanisms are optional. Security issues depend on the underlying authentication mechanism chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: AUTH is just one option. If it does not work, mail programs can try a different secret game or use the old plain password method as a backup.

references.text: Myers, J., "IMAP4 Authentication Mechanisms", RFC 1731, December 1994.
Siemborski, R. and A. Melnikov, "The Post Office Protocol (POP3) Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) Authentication Mechanism", RFC 5034, July 2007.
